questions.question: Which of the following is not used in note making?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Date

Note making uses a **title, headings and sub-headings, abbreviations, symbols and indentation** to record the main ideas compactly. A **date** has nothing to do with the content of notes — it neither shortens them nor shows their structure.

questions.question: While writing a notice, where do we place the name of the institution/organisation?
questions.answer:
**(C)** At the top

The **name of the institution or organisation is written at the very top, in capitals**, and only then the word NOTICE, the date, the heading and the body. The notice speaks in the institution's name, so the institution is named first.

questions.question: What would be the correct way of writing the date in letter writing?
questions.answer:
**(D)** 1st February, 2025

The date in a letter is written in **words** — "1st February, 2025" (or "February 1, 2025") — never in numerals. Numerals such as 01/02/2025 are read differently in different countries (1 February in India, 2 January in the United States), and a formal letter should admit no such doubt.

questions.question: How should an article be ended?
questions.answer:
**(A)** With a suitable conclusion

An article ends with a **conclusion** — a summing-up, an opinion or a suggestion that closes the argument begun in the opening paragraph. Greetings and thanks belong to a speech, since an article is read, not heard.

questions.question: In Report Writing, the narration of the event is always written in
questions.answer:
**(C)** the immediate past tense

A report describes an event that has just taken place, so the narration is in the **past tense** — "the function began at 10 a.m.", "the Chief Guest planted a sapling". "Immediate" because the event is recent, and the report reads like a first account of it.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of summary writing?
options: Summary being shorter than the text
questions.answer:
**(B)** Exact words from the text

A summary **states the main ideas in your own words**, omitting examples, repetitions and details, and is always **shorter than the original**. Copying the exact words of the text is not summarizing but quoting.

questions.question: Which country was defeated in the Franco-Prussian War?
questions.answer:
**(A)** France

In the **Franco-Prussian War (1870–71) France was defeated by Prussia**, and Alsace and Lorraine passed into German hands. That is why the order comes from Berlin that only German shall be taught in the schools of Alsace — the fact behind M. Hamel's last lesson.

questions.question: What do 'you boys' appear like to the author in the story 'Lost Spring'?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Morning birds

Anees Jung tells the ragpicker children, "**You are like the morning birds** who have forgotten to go home" — a phrase of tenderness and reproach at once, for children who should be at school and at play but are out in the streets at dawn, hunting through garbage.

questions.question: Gandhiji and Shukla boarded a train in Calcutta for
questions.answer:
**(B)** Patna

From Calcutta "**they boarded a train for Patna**", and from Patna they went on to Champaran. It was on the way that Gandhi stopped at Muzaffarpur to meet Professor J. B. Kripalani and to gather the peasants' stories before facing the landlords.

questions.question: What made Bama shriek with laughter?
options: Looking at an old man holding the packet by its string
questions.answer:
**(D)** looking at an old man holding a packet by its string

On her way home Bama saw an **elderly man from the untouchable community** carrying a small packet of food "**by its string**", not touching it, because his touch would pollute the upper-caste man who was to receive it. The sight struck her as so absurd that she "shrieked with laughter" — and then her brother Anan explained it, and the laughter turned to shame.

questions.question: 'Can a God-given lineage ever be broken?' Who said these words?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Mukesh's grandmother

Mukesh's **old grandmother** says this. She has never seen a full meal in her life and accepts the family's trade as destiny: the bangle-making is "**a God-given lineage**" that cannot be broken. It is against exactly this fatalism that Mukesh's wish to be a motor mechanic sets itself.

questions.question: 'Deep Water' is an excerpt from
questions.answer:
**(C)** 'Of Men and Mountains'

"Deep Water" is taken from **William O. Douglas's autobiography *Of Men and Mountains*** (1950). The chapter is his account of the two drownings that gave him his fear of water and of the long, deliberate campaign by which he defeated it.

questions.question: The magistrate asked Gandhiji to furnish bail for those ................ minutes.
questions.answer:
**(D)** 120

When Gandhi refused to leave Motihari on the collector's orders, he was served with a notice and told to appear in court, where the magistrate asked him to furnish bail for **two hours (120 minutes)** while he considered the case. Gandhi refused, pleaded guilty, and asked for the heaviest penalty — the beginning of his civil disobedience in Champaran.

questions.question: Which game did the peddler and the old man play?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Mjolis

The crofter and the peddler played "**mjolis**" — a Swedish card game something like rummy — on Christmas Eve. The game matters because it is the moment of **trust and company**: the old man shares his cards, his porridge and his talk with a stranger who is already planning to rob him.

questions.question: Which brand's make-up material was used in Gemini Studios?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Pancake

The make-up material used at the Gemini Studios was of the brand "**Pancake**" — thick, greasy and applied under blazing lights. The chapter opens with the office boy carrying those tins, and the brand gives the chapter its title.

questions.question: Sophie told Geoff that Danny was unable to sign an autograph for her because
options: He was in a hurry to go home
questions.answer:
**(C)** he said he would do it later

Sophie invents the excuse: Danny "**said he'd do it later**" — next time. The invention is the story's quiet joke: she has to keep the meeting alive in her brother's eyes, and the promise of a future autograph does it, though no autograph will ever come.

questions.question: Kamala Das was driving from the house of
questions.answer:
**(A)** her parents

The poet is driving **from her parents' home** to Cochin airport: she has been visiting her ageing mother, and the poem records the last look at her face in the car before the parting. (*The solved booklet ticks "her in-laws"; the poem says the poet is going home from her parents' house.*)

questions.question: What is a 'bower' in the poem 'A Thing of Beauty'?
questions.answer:
**(C)** a pleasant place

A **bower** is a shady, sheltered place under trees — a **pleasant, restful spot**. Keats writes of "**a bower quiet for us**", where beauty gives us "sleep full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing". It is not a shrine or a crowd, but a place of calm.

questions.question: What does the poet ask us to do while he counts up to twelve?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Keep quiet

Neruda asks us to "**keep still**" and to "**count to twelve**" in a moment of silence in which we "**would not speak in any language**". The counting is a device for the pause: the poem's whole hope lies in that interval of stillness before the world starts again.

questions.question: Why did the house owner put up a new shed?
options: To keep an eye on the rich car owners
questions.answer:
**(B)** To earn some money

The country folk put up the "little new shed" **to sell their produce** — "wild berries", "golden squash" — to the cars that pass, and so to "**feel**" a little of the city money in their hands. It is a hope of earning, not begging and not spying on the traffic.

questions.question: How are the tigers described in the poem 'Aunt Jennifer's Tigers'?
questions.answer:
**(C)** fearless

The tigers are "**sleek and elegant**" and "**fearless**": they "do not fear the men beneath the tree". (*The solved booklet ticks "all of these"; the poem itself applies the word "fearless" to them, while "chivalric" describes Aunt Jennifer's knightly hunters and "ferocious" nobody.*)

questions.question: Who is the Tiger King?
questions.answer:
**(A)** the Maharaja of Pratibandapuram

The Tiger King is the **Maharaja of Pratibandapuram**, whose full title Kalki lists at preposterous length — "His Highness Jamedar-General, Khiledar-Major, Sata Vyaghra Samhari..." — and who is known to the world as the Tiger King for killing ninety-nine tigers.

questions.question: In which hour was the prince of 'The Tiger King' born?
questions.answer:
**(A)** In the hour of the bull

The astrologers, after reading the stars, announced that the prince was born "**in the hour of the bull**" — and that as the bull and the tiger are enemies, death would come to him "from the Tiger". That single phrase governs the whole of the Maharaja's life.

questions.question: Who was Sam in 'The Third Level'?
options: A psychiatrist and a friend of Charley
questions.answer:
**(B)** a psychiatrist and a friend of Charley

Sam was Charley's **psychiatrist friend**, who explained the third level as "a waking-dream wish to escape", and who then bought eight hundred dollars' worth of old currency and vanished into Galesburg of 1894 — sending Charley the first day cover as proof.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: How many time zones did Tishani Doshi cross?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Nine

To reach Antarctica from India, Tishani Doshi crossed "**nine time zones**" — she says the journey took her from Chennai to the Antarctic, "crossing nine time zones" in the process, which is part of why the continent feels like another planet.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: Which programme was headed by the Canadian Geoff Green?
questions.answer:
**(A)** Students on Ice

**Geoff Green**, a Canadian, founded "**Students on Ice**", the programme that takes school and college students to the polar regions so that they may see for themselves the "icebergs as big as countries" and understand the earth's fragility. Tishani Doshi travelled with it.

questions.question: Who was Dr. Sadao?
questions.answer:
**(A)** a Japanese doctor

**Dr. Sadao Hoki** is a **Japanese surgeon** — "the best surgeon in Japan", the old General's personal physician, who had studied surgery and medicine in America and whose house stands on the coast near a prison camp.

questions.question: How old is Derry?
questions.answer:
**(D)** fourteen

Derry tells Mr. Lamb, "**I'm fourteen**". He is a boy of fourteen whose face was burnt by acid when he was a child, and who has spent years expecting people to look away from him.

questions.question: What did Mr. Lamb make of apples?
questions.answer:
**(C)** jelly

Mr. Lamb explains that he makes "**jelly**" from his apples — that is why he asks Derry to help him pick them. The jelly is a small emblem of his philosophy: a man with one leg and a garden full of fruit still makes something sweet out of what he has.

questions.question: Who was Anan?
questions.answer:
**(D)** Bama's elder brother

**Anan** is Bama's **elder brother**, the one who explains to her why the old man carried the packet by its string, and who tells her that "**we too are human beings**". It is he who teaches her that education is the way to "touch" the world without being polluted by its prejudice.

questions.question:
Read the passage on Naren's birthday and answer any six of the following:
(a) Why was there great excitement at the Dutta's house?
(b) What were the clothes bought for Naren?
(c) What did he see outside the window?
(d) What did he do after seeing outside?
(e) Why did the mother scold Naren?
(f) What was the name of Naren's father?
(g) What words of Naren's mother came true?
(h) Find the similar words from the passage which mean (i) smell (ii) charity.
questions.answer:
### (a)

**Answer.** Because it was **12 January, Little Naren's birthday**, and the house was **decorated with flowers**. In the kitchen "the delicious aroma of the feast" was rising, and **relatives and friends had been invited**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "There was a great excitement at Vishwanath Dutta's house. It was the 12th January, Little Naren's birthday. The house was decorated with flowers."

**The occasion.** A birthday in a well-to-do Bengali household of the time meant new clothes, a feast, guests and a freshly bathed child saying his prayers — all of which the passage describes in its first two paragraphs.

### (b)

**Answer.** Naren was given a **silk dhoti and kurta, and a warm shawl** — "exactly like clothes his father wore to the court".

**The passage's own words.**

> "It was just what he had wanted! A silk dhoti and kurta and a warm shawl, exactly like clothes his father wore to the court."

**Why it matters.** The clothes are the boy's pride: he combs his hair carefully and, "**proud as a peacock**", struts before the huge mirror. It is precisely this new shawl, kurta and dhoti that he throws out of the window a little later.

### (c)

**Answer.** He saw "**a wretched family shivering in the cold**" and heard a **beggar calling for alms**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "While he was admiring himself, he heard a beggar calling for alms. He ran to the window, and saw a wretched family shivering in the cold."

**What it did to him.** "As he heard their sad and painful cries, it **pierced his heart**." The contrast is the story's point: a boy admiring his new silk clothes at a mirror, and a family with nothing, in the January cold, just outside the same window.

### (d)

**Answer.** He "**quickly opened the window**" and **threw down his shawl**; "then followed his kurta and the dhoti". He gave away the new clothes he had been so proud of a moment before.

**The passage's own words.**

> "Quickly he opened the window and took off the shawl and threw it down. Then followed his kurta and the dhoti."

**What followed.** His mother came in and found him "**dressed in his old clothes**". His explanation was simply, "they were shivering in the cold so I..."; her scolding and her prophecy ("In this way you will become a monk") close the passage.

### (e)

**Answer.** Because he had **given away his brand-new birthday clothes** to a beggar family, and she thought such reckless charity would ruin him: "**Will you give away everything just because someone needs it?**"

**The passage's own words.**

> "The mother scolded, 'Will you give away everything just because someone needs it'. In this way you will become a monk."

**The irony.** The scolding is a prophecy: Naren grew up to be **Swami Vivekananda**, who "gave up the world to serve the poor". The mother's complaint that he would "become a monk" is exactly what came true, and the passage ends by saying so.

### (f)

**Answer.** **Vishwanath Dutta.**

**The passage's own words.**

> "There was a great excitement at Vishwanath Dutta's house."

**Why the name is given.** He was a successful Calcutta lawyer, and the passage mentions him for two reasons: the house and the feast are his, and it is "his father's" court clothes that Naren's new silk dhoti, kurta and shawl are compared to.

### (g)

**Answer.** Her words "**In this way you will become a monk**" came true.

**The passage's own words.**

> "The mother scolded, 'Will you give away everything just because someone needs it'. In this way you will become a monk."

> "Naren's mother's words were to come true. Naren gave up the world to serve the poor and today we know him as Swami Vivekananda."

**The point.** What the mother said in irritation at a spoiled birthday turned out to be prophecy: the boy who threw his new clothes to a shivering family became the monk who gave up everything for the poor.

### (h)

**Answer.** (a) smell — **aroma**; (b) charity — **alms**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "...came the delicious **aroma** of the feast that was being prepared..."

> "...he heard a beggar calling for **alms**."

**Note.** Both words are the passage's own. "Aroma" is a pleasant smell (of food); "alms" are the money or food given to the poor — the concrete form of charity.

questions.question:
Read the following passage carefully and make notes on it, using headings, sub-headings and abbreviations. Give a suitable title.

There are a number of reasons why we must conserve the world's plants and animals. Plants are essential for our own survival. Only they can use the sun's energy to make food. So, plants are the vital first link in the food chain of which we ourselves form part. One of the by-products of the food making process in plants is oxygen, without which very few forms of life can exist on earth.

Animals need plants in order to survive, but plants also need animals. All animals and plants are bound together in delicately balanced communities or ecosystems. The removal of just one species can drastically alter a whole ecosystem.

Our own survival may be threatened if we cause too much disruption to the natural processes that occur in this planet. The destruction of the world's rain forest is causing some concern in this respect. In some areas the removal of the rain forest has already reduced the local rainfall. Some scientists suggest that if too much forest is destroyed, the rainfall in crop-growing areas will decrease, and these areas will become deserts.

Another important reason for preserving wildlife is that it is a potentially inexhaustible natural resource. We use many plants and animals to supply us with food, materials and chemicals. If we exploit these species to the points at which they cannot replenish themselves, they will no longer be available to us. At the moment we understand the biology of only a tiny fraction of the world's wildlife. We do not know what useful materials we will lose in this destruction.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: Why We Must Conserve Wildlife**

**1. Plants — the base of life**
   1.1 essential for human survival
   1.2 only plants convert sun's energy into food
   1.3 first link in the food chain (we form part of it)
   1.4 food-making gives off O₂ — needed by almost all life

**2. Interdependence of plants & animals**
   2.1 animals need plants; plants also need animals
   2.2 bound in delicately balanced ecosystems
   2.3 loss of one species → whole ecosystem drastically altered

**3. Danger to our own survival**
   3.1 too much disruption of natural processes = threat
   3.2 e.g. destruction of rain forests
   3.3 already reduced local rainfall in some areas
   3.4 scientists: more forest loss → less rain in crop areas → deserts

**4. Wildlife as a natural resource**
   4.1 potentially inexhaustible resource
   4.2 supplies food, materials, chemicals
   4.3 over-exploitation → species cannot replenish → lost for ever
   4.4 we know only a tiny fraction of wildlife biology → unknown losses

**Abbreviations used:** O₂ = oxygen; e.g. = for example; → = leads to; & = and; consvn = conservation; spp. = species.

**Note on the form.** Notes are written in **phrases, not sentences**, in a **numbered outline** with indentation for sub-points, and with **standard abbreviations and symbols**. A title is compulsory, and nothing that is not in the passage should be added.

questions.question: Write a summary of the passage given in Q. 39 in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Plants must be conserved because they alone convert the sun's energy into food, forming the first link of the food chain, and release the oxygen almost all life needs. Plants and animals are bound in delicately balanced ecosystems, so the loss of even one species can alter the whole. Destroying rain forests may reduce rainfall and turn croplands into desert. Wildlife also supplies food, materials and chemicals; over-exploited species vanish before we have even understood them.

**The summary in one sentence.** We must conserve plants and animals because our food, our oxygen, our climate and our survival itself depend on the balance between them.

**Note on the form.** A summary keeps **only the main ideas, in your own words, in one paragraph**, in about the number of words asked for, with no examples beyond the one the passage itself stresses, no quotation and no personal opinion.

questions.question: Which was the first incident when Douglas was almost drowned and developed aversion for water? (Answer in about 50 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** At three or four, on a beach in **California**, Douglas was knocked down and buried by the waves. "They swept over me... I was buried in water", and when he came up his breath was gone and he was "**paralysed with fear**" — the first step in his aversion to water.

**Why it lasted.** The memory of that "**mammoth wave**" prepared the ground for the terror at the YMCA pool years later.

questions.question: Why did Rajkumar Shukla take Gandhiji to Champaran? (Answer in about 50 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Shukla, an **illiterate but resolute sharecropper**, took Gandhi to Champaran **to get justice for the peasants** who were forced to grow indigo on part of their land and surrender the harvest as rent, and then made to pay to be released from the arrangement when synthetic indigo ruined the crop.

**How he did it.** He followed Gandhi from Lucknow to Cawnpore, Calcutta and Patna until he agreed to come.

questions.question: What do the parting words 'see you soon Amma' of the poetess and her smile signify? (Answer in about 50 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** They signify a **brave disguise for fear**. The poet has just seen her mother's face "ashen like that of a corpse", and she says "see you soon, amma" with a smile so as to hide her old familiar ache — the fear of losing her.

**The irony.** The cheerful words are a hope, not a promise, and the smile is a mask.

questions.question: Who was Tom? How did Sadao help him to escape? (Answer in about 50 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Tom** is the wounded **American prisoner of war** — a young man of about twenty-five, shot and thrown up on the beach near Sadao's house, whom the doctor saves and hides.

**How he escaped.** Sadao gave him **his own boat, clothes, food, water and a flashlight** and sent him to a **deserted island**, to wait for a Korean fishing boat.

questions.question: Who is Bama? How did she learn about untouchability? (Answer in about 50 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Bama is a **Tamil Dalit writer**, the narrator of "We Too Are Human Beings". She learnt about untouchability at about eleven, when she saw an **elderly untouchable carrying a packet by its string** and laughed — and her **brother Anan explained** that the man's touch would pollute the upper castes.

**What she felt.** Shame, and a new resolve to study and break that "**God-given**" order.

questions.question: Describe what little Franz saw along the way when he walked to school that day. (Answer in 80–100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Franz set out very late and afraid of M. Hamel's questions on participles, and he thought of **running away and spending the day out of doors**, for the day was warm and bright.

**On the way** he saw the **Prussians drilling** in the open field behind the sawmill, and he saw a crowd in front of the **bulletin board** by the town hall. **Old Hauser**, with his three-cornered hat, was there reading the notice, and Wachter the blacksmith mocked the boy, "Don't go so fast, bub!"

**Franz's thought.** He wondered at the blacksmith's words, but he hurried on to school, where the unusual silence and M. Hamel's dress told him that something was wrong.

questions.question: Mukesh's family was caught in the 'web of poverty' and the 'stigma of caste'. Explain in detail. (Answer in 80–100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Mukesh's family are **bangle makers of Firozabad**, and in that town the two fetters hold a whole people.

**The web of poverty.** His grandmother has "not seen a full meal in her life"; his father has **gone blind** from the dust of the glass furnaces; the family lives in a "half-built shack" where the bangle-maker works beside his cooking fire. A cycle of **debt, sahukars, policemen and middlemen** keeps them from ever keeping the profit of their own labour.

**The stigma of caste.** Because they are **born into the bangle-makers' caste**, they are not allowed any other trade: the author notes that the children are told it is "**his kismet**", and that to try another work would invite the punishment of the "**sahukars**" and the "**police**".

**The one crack in the wall.** Mukesh says he will be a motor mechanic — the author's single hope in the chapter.

questions.question: You are Govinda/Gaurika, the head boy/girl of S. S. +2 High School, Lapung. Your school is organising a tour to Nainital. Write a notice inviting students who are willing to go on the tour, in not more than 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**S. S. +2 HIGH SCHOOL, LAPUNG**

**NOTICE**

*12 November 2025*

**TOUR TO NAINITAL**

A five-day educational tour to **Nainital** is being organised in the winter break. Students of Classes XI and XII who wish to join should give their names, with the consent of their parents, to the undersigned by **20 November**. The cost and the itinerary will be announced on 22 November.

**Gaurika**
Head Girl

**Keep it short.** In a 50-word notice give **what, where, when, the last date and whom to contact** — and nothing else. Signature with designation closes it.

questions.question: Your college is raising funds for the homeless and poor people. You are Devdas/Dolly, the Secretary of the Cultural Club of St. Francis School, Khalari. Write a notice requesting students to donate, in not more than 50 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**ST. FRANCIS SCHOOL, KHALARI**

**NOTICE**

*20 December 2025*

**DONATIONS FOR THE HOMELESS**

The Cultural Club is collecting money, clothes and blankets for the **homeless and the poor of Khalari** this winter. Students may put their contribution in the box outside the school office by **24 December**. Please give generously.

**Devdas**
Secretary, Cultural Club

**Keep it short.** In 50 words: the **cause, what is wanted, where and by when to give it**, and the request — with the signature and the office held.

questions.question: You are Tulika/Tarun. Write a letter to the Editor of 'The Express', Ranchi, complaining about the frequent breakdown in the supply of electricity in your village. (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Village Bero**
**P.O. Bero, Ranchi**
**14 July 2025**

The Editor
*The Express*
Ranchi

**Subject: Frequent breakdown of electricity supply in Bero village**

Sir

Through your columns I wish to draw the attention of the electricity department to the **frequent breakdown of power supply in Bero village**.

There is a power cut for six to eight hours every day, and for the last three weeks the supply has failed altogether after 7 p.m. The transformer near the temple has not been repaired for two years. Students cannot study for their examinations, the tubewell cannot run, and two families have had their fans and a refrigerator burnt by the surge when the supply returns.

I request the department to repair the transformer, replace the old cables and publish a maintenance schedule.

Yours faithfully
**Tarun**

**Format points.** Address and date, addressee, subject, the **complaint with specific instances and consequences**, and a clear request — in about 100 words.

questions.question: Your school observed 'Save Water Day'. You were a participant in that awareness programme. Write a brief report in about 125–150 words to be published in your school magazine. You are Ram/Rani of Marwari +2 High School, Ranchi. (Answer in about 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**SAVE WATER DAY OBSERVED AT MARWARI +2 HIGH SCHOOL**

*By Rani, Class XII*

**Ranchi, 22 March 2025.** "Save Water Day" was observed at Marwari +2 High School, Ranchi on 22 March with a **morning assembly, a poster exhibition and a rally through the neighbouring lanes**, the programme running from 8 a.m. to noon.

**The programme.** The Principal opened the day with a short speech on the falling water table of Ranchi, after which the science teacher, Mr. Sinha, demonstrated how a leaking tap wastes forty litres a day. Students of Classes IX to XII then displayed **sixty posters** in the corridor, and the best three were given prizes. At 10.30 a.m. about two hundred students walked in a **rally** through the lanes around the school, carrying placards reading "Save every drop" and explaining to shopkeepers how to harvest rainwater.

**The pledge.** The day ended with an **oath** in the assembly: to close every tap, to report every leak, and to waste no water at home. The Principal announced that a **rainwater harvesting pit** would be dug in the school compound before the monsoon.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, place and date, the **sequence of the programme**, the numbers and a closing resolve — in the past tense, without personal comment.

questions.question: Write an article on 'Need for Hygiene to fight diseases at the present situation'. (Answer in about 150 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**CLEAN HANDS, FEWER DISEASES**

The cheapest medicine in the world is soap and water. At a time when new infections keep appearing and hospitals are crowded, the plainest defence is still **hygiene** — and it costs almost nothing.

**Why it matters now.** Most of the fevers that fill our villages' clinics — diarrhoea, typhoid, cholera, jaundice — travel through water and food that have been touched by dirty hands. A single handwash with soap before a meal can cut that traffic drastically. In towns, the danger is the garbage heap at the corner, the choked drain and the stagnant water in which mosquitoes breed; in villages, it is the open defecation and the uncovered well.

**What must be done.** Wash hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet; keep drinking water covered; refuse to let garbage collect near the house; use a toilet and keep it clean; and take the full course of any medicine prescribed. Schools must teach this, and panchayats must keep the drains and the water sources clean.

**The lesson.** Epidemics are fought in the home, not only in the hospital. Hygiene is a habit, and habits can be taught.

**Format points.** A title, the **problem, the causes and consequences, and a set of practical remedies**, with a short, firm conclusion — within 150 words.
